live.name: GOLD HARVEST
live.headline: GOLD HARVEST: a threat actor tracked under several names
live.in_short: The catalogue lists GOLD HARVEST under five other names and names three remote-access tools tied to it. No public report in this library describes its operations.

sentences.t: The catalogue record, sourced to Secureworks, tracks the actor as GOLD HARVEST.
The same record lists these aliases: Octo Tempest, Roasted 0ktapus, Scatter Swine, Scattered Spider and UNC3944.
The record lists three tools: AnyDesk, ConnectWise Control and Logmein.
No public report in this library describes its operations.

next.name: GOLD HARVEST
next.headline: GOLD HARVEST (Scattered Spider): a social-engineering crew that goes after help desks and outsourced IT
next.in_short: GOLD HARVEST, better known as Scattered Spider, is a financially motivated group. Vendors describe it as using phone and help-desk tricks to get in, and as working with ransomware operators and allied groups.

sentences.t: The Secureworks catalogue lists GOLD HARVEST under several other names: Octo Tempest, Roasted 0ktapus, Scatter Swine, Scattered Spider and UNC3944.
CrowdStrike describes Scattered Spider as a prolific eCrime adversary that has run financially motivated activity since early 2022.
Check Point's overview, drawn from public intelligence, says the group is composed primarily of young people aged 19 to 22 from the US and UK.
ReliaQuest calls it a financially motivated gang associated with the hacking collective known as The Com.
CrowdStrike says early campaigns reportedly hit customer relationship management and business-process outsourcing firms, plus telecommunications and technology companies.
ReliaQuest reports that 70% of the group's targets sit in technology, finance and retail trade.

Halcyon says the group compromises call centres and other outsourcing providers to reach many clients at once. It assesses that recent UK retail and US insurance attacks likely began, at least in part, this way.
Check Point says the group is now also targeting aviation. It notes the link to airline attacks rests on media reports and advisories.
Resecurity says the group is known for help desk impersonation and credential theft, and pioneered SIM swapping and MFA bombing to get past multi-factor checks.
ReliaQuest says the group relies on phishing frameworks such as Evilginx and on vishing, which is phone-based phishing, to bypass multi-factor authentication.
Halcyon says the group has consistently used insider recruitment and has been linked to driver-abuse (BYOVD) and EDR-evasion techniques.

The catalogue lists AnyDesk, ConnectWise Control and Logmein among its tools. Halcyon says the group guides users through downloading remote access tools such as AnyDesk or ScreenConnect while posing as IT staff.
ReliaQuest says the group has alliances with ransomware operators ALPHV, RansomHub and DragonForce.
Sygnia names Scattered Spider among groups that attack VMware ESXi virtualisation environments. CrowdStrike says the group used an open-source proxy tool on compromised vCenter servers.
BleepingComputer's report says the group breached MGM Resorts in September 2023 by impersonating an employee, then encrypted over 100 VMware ESXi hypervisors with BlackCat ransomware.
ReliaQuest notes a wave of attacks on UK retailers in May 2025, including Marks & Spencer, Co-op and Harrods. It says nothing definitive has tied them to the group.
The Aflac breach disclosure was reported as showing all the signs of a Scattered Spider attack, though an Aflac spokesperson could not attribute it to a specific group.
Trustwave SpiderLabs reads "Scattered LAPSUS$ Hunters", a brand that appeared on Telegram in August 2025, as a situational alliance and not a formal merger.
EclecticIQ assesses that ShinyHunters is very likely relying on members of Scattered Spider and The Com to carry out voice phishing attacks.

Rapid7 described an April 2026 intrusion that began with a Microsoft Teams message from a fake IT Support account. It says this mirrors Octo Tempest-style tradecraft, and does not present it as a confirmed link.
Treat password and MFA reset requests to the help desk as high-risk, and verify the caller's identity by a separate, trusted channel.
Hold outsourced IT and support providers to the same access controls and monitoring as internal staff.
